name: The Devil
upright: Identity proven with the right factors: phishing-resistant MFA, tickets bound to synced clocks, sessions that expire on time.
reversed: Reused passwords, prompts approved just to stop the buzzing, stolen hashes replayed and sessions that never end.
vision: A horned figure squats on a pedestal, collecting three gifts at the door: a whispered word, a carried coin and a fingerprint; three whispered words buy nothing. Below, two chained figures tap yes on a box that buzzes all night, never noticing that their chains are loose enough to lift. The horned one tries one stolen key on a thousand doors and opens others with only a wax print of a key. At the back gate a three-headed dog stamps tickets with the hour and burns any five minutes off; a thief who stole its seal prints golden tickets. The inverted torch drips two flames: one shuts out friends, one admits strangers.
decode: Word, coin, fingerprint; three words buy nothing → MFA mixes factor types: something you know, have, are. A password plus a security question is still one factor.
Tapping yes on a box that buzzes all night; chains loose enough to lift → MFA fatigue: push prompts spammed until one is approved. Number matching breaks the spell.
One stolen key on a thousand doors; a wax print of a key → credential stuffing replays breached passwords on other sites; pass-the-hash replays the hash itself.
The dog stamping tickets with the hour; golden tickets → Kerberos tickets need clocks within 5 minutes; a stolen KRBTGT hash lets an attacker forge any TGT.
Two flames of the inverted torch → type I errors (FRR) shut out valid users; type II (FAR) admit impostors. Where the rates cross is the CER: lower is better.
facts: Kerberos uses symmetric keys, not PKI: the KDC holds every principal's secret key, so it is a single point of failure. The password itself never crosses the network.
Kerberoasting: any domain user requests service tickets for accounts with SPNs and cracks them offline; long random or managed service-account passwords defeat it.
Session IDs must be random, sent only over TLS and regenerated at login, with idle and absolute timeouts; a stolen session cookie walks straight past MFA.
trap: The collective believed any MFA stops phishing. A fake page can relay passwords and one-time codes in real time; only origin-bound FIDO2/WebAuthn keys refuse to answer the wrong site.
